article_title: What Further Research Is Needed on Restorative Justice in Schools?
citation: Hurley, N., Guckenburg, S., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). What Further Research is Needed on Restorative Justice in Schools? WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Implement restorative justice with all adults in the school before implementing it with students
description: For whole-school RJ models, the article reports experts encourage a sequencing principle: build RJ practice among all adults in the school — "teachers, bus drivers, cafeteria staff, administrators, specialists" — before introducing it with students. Experts also note RJ is most successfully implemented when students, school employees, parents and guardians, and community members all embrace it, and that proper implementation requires understanding the school climate and the nature and source of the school's issues beforehand.
requirements: A clear understanding of the school climate and of the nature, extent, and source of the issues the school contends with before implementing RJ
constraints: Stated by experts for whole-school models; the article presents it as expert advice, not a tested finding
target_learners: all school adults including teachers, bus drivers, cafeteria staff, administrators, and specialists
target_learning_goals: school-wide adoption of non-punitive, relationship-restoring disciplinary practice
examples: Experts recommended implementing RJ with all adults in the school first when a whole-school model is desired
key_sources: Hurley, N., Guckenburg, S., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). What Further Research is Needed on Restorative Justice in Schools? WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED559727

article_title: Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: Summary Findings from Interviews with Experts
citation: Guckenburg, S., Hurley, N., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: Summary Findings from Interviews with Experts. San Francisco: WestEd. http://jprc.wested.org/
title: Four key features define restorative justice in schools per expert consensus
description: The report distills expert interviews into four defining features of RJ in schools: "Focus on repairing harm rather than punishing the offender," including student voice, a whole-school approach, and building students' social/emotional skills. RJ is described as rebuilding relationships and collaboratively solving problems rather than punishing offenders, with circles exemplifying how student voice is valued.
requirements: Trained facilitators conduct RJ circles so all participants can hear about and understand the harm from different points of view
constraints: The report notes RJ is difficult to define and that measuring fidelity of implementation requires tools still in the development stage
target_learners: K-12 students in U.S. elementary and secondary schools
key_sources: Guckenburg, S., Hurley, N., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: Summary Findings from Interviews with Experts. San Francisco: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED568378

article_title: Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: Summary Findings from Interviews with Experts
citation: Guckenburg, S., Hurley, N., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: Summary Findings from Interviews with Experts. San Francisco: WestEd. http://jprc.wested.org/
title: Five specific restorative justice practices implement RJ goals in schools
description: Experts identified specific program components intended to achieve RJ goals: restorative circles, restorative conferencing, peace rooms, restorative questioning, and active listening. Circles are "facilitated meetings that allow students and others to come together for problem solving, resolving disciplinary issues, receiving content instruction, and discussing concerns related to difficult topics."
requirements: Facilitation and, in some schools, dedicated "peace rooms" as safe spaces where circles and conferences may be held
constraints: Some labeled-restorative strategies, such as peer courts and peer juries, are considered inconsistent with RJ philosophy by some experts because they focus on the offender rather than the victim
examples: Circles use a talking piece so only the holder may speak; peace rooms provide safe space for circles and conferences
key_sources: Guckenburg, S., Hurley, N., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: Summary Findings from Interviews with Experts. San Francisco: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED568378

article_title: Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: An Updated Research Review
citation: Fronius, Darling-Hammond, Persson, Guckenburg, Hurley, & Petrosino. (2019). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: An Updated Research Review. WestEd Justice & Prevention Research Center. http://jprc.wested.org/
title: Reintegrative shaming, procedural justice, and defiance theory as theoretical frameworks underlying restorative justice in schools
description: The review organizes RJ's theoretical grounding around three accounts. Reintegrative shaming theory distinguishes shaming that leads to "reconciliation with and reacceptance of the wrongdoer" from stigmatizing shaming that isolates the offender. Procedural justice holds that giving students voice in decision-making leads them to view institutional power as more legitimate and fair. Defiance theory warns that absent perceived legitimacy and fairness, young people may respond with defiance and future infractions. Together these frameworks support RJ's potential for stronger school community and fewer behavioral issues.
requirements: Educators must be able to recognize how to use shame as a path toward reintegration rather than stigmatization, a line the review notes is fine and easily crossed
constraints: Critics argue reintegrative shaming may have unintended harmful effects in school settings (Vaandering, 2010, as cited in the review)
target_learners: K-12 students in U.S. primary and secondary schools
target_learning_goals: Increased student perceptions of fairness and legitimacy of school discipline, greater compliance, and stronger school community
examples: The review describes reintegrative shaming materializing as direct actions such as requiring a student to publicly apologize, or indirect actions such as a teacher expressing disappointment to a student's parent.
key_sources: Fronius, Darling-Hammond, Persson, Guckenburg, Hurley, & Petrosino. (2019). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: An Updated Research Review. WestEd Justice & Prevention Research Center. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED595733

article_title: Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: An Updated Research Review
citation: Fronius, Darling-Hammond, Persson, Guckenburg, Hurley, & Petrosino. (2019). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: An Updated Research Review. WestEd Justice & Prevention Research Center. http://jprc.wested.org/
title: Restorative justice implementation guides and toolkits for schools and districts
description: The review compiles a table of publicly available guides and toolkits that "provide more information on the steps to consider when starting an RJ program in a school or district." These include The Advancement Project's educator guide (2014), the Denver School-Based Restorative Practices Partnership's step-by-step guide (2017), Kidde & Alfred's Alameda County working guide (2011), the Restorative Interventions Implementation Toolkit (Beckman, McMorris, & Gower, 2012), and the Oakland Unified School District whole-school implementation guide (2014), each with a printed source URL.
requirements: Administrators and educators need access to the tools and resources necessary to successfully fund, implement, and evaluate their RJ program
constraints: The review notes the implementation steps these resources describe are not backed by rigorous scientific evidence such as randomized controlled trials
target_learners: K-12 school and district administrators and educators implementing RJ programs
target_learning_goals: Funding, implementing, and sustaining restorative justice programs in schools and districts
examples: The review's Table 1 lists five resources with authors, years, and source URLs, including the Oakland Unified School District Restorative Justice Implementation Guide: A Whole School Approach.
key_sources: Fronius, Darling-Hammond, Persson, Guckenburg, Hurley, & Petrosino. (2019). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: An Updated Research Review. WestEd Justice & Prevention Research Center. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED595733

article_title: Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: A Research Review
citation: Fronius, Persson, Guckenburg, Hurley, & Petrosino. (2016). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: A Research Review. WestEd. http://jprc.wested.org
title: Restorative justice theoretical frameworks: reintegrative shaming, procedural justice, and defiance theory
description: The review organizes RJ's theoretical basis around three accounts. Reintegrative shaming (Braithwaite) shames wrongdoing while reintegrating the offender into the community rather than isolating them; procedural justice (Tyler) holds that giving students voice in decision-making increases perceived legitimacy and compliance; and defiance theory links perceived illegitimacy and unfairness to defiance and future infractions. Together, "The perspectives of reintegrative shaming, procedural justice, and defiance theory all support the potential of RJ in leading to a stronger school community, better climate, and fewer behavioral issues." The review uses these frameworks to explain why RJ might reduce punitive discipline while building relationships.
requirements: Educators must be able to use shame as a path toward reintegration rather than stigmatization, which the review says educators may not always recognize
constraints: Critics argue reintegrative shaming may have unintended harmful effects in school settings (Vaandering, 2010); there is a fine line between supportive and stigmatizing shame
target_learners: K-12 students in U.S. primary and secondary schools
target_learning_goals: Building positive school climate, student accountability, and behavioral self-regulation through relationship repair
examples: The review describes reintegrative shaming materializing as direct actions such as requiring a public apology or indirect actions such as a teacher expressing disappointment to a parent
key_sources: Fronius, Persson, Guckenburg, Hurley, & Petrosino. (2016). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: A Research Review. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED596786

article_title: Digital innovations in teacher recruitment: An experimental study
citation: Klassen, Robert Mark, Wang, Hui, Cutting, Joe, Thompson-Lee, Sophie, Snell, Rebecca J.S., See, Beng Huat, Saiger, Michael. (2025). Digital innovations in teacher recruitment: An experimental study. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105450
title: Realistic job preview (RJP): four animated classroom scenarios with response rating and expert feedback
description: The RJP intervention consisted of "four animated classroom scenarios" presenting balanced, authentic depictions of workplace situations. For each scenario, participants viewed a video-based classroom scenario, rated the appropriateness of three possible responses to a dilemma, wrote a reflective rationale, and read real-time feedback comparing their ratings with experienced teachers' ratings. Participants then received one of four fit messages based on score congruence with experts.
requirements: Content built in collaboration with practicing teachers to enhance believability and authenticity
A scoring key established through previous work with subject matter experts
key_sources: Klassen, Robert Mark, Wang, Hui, Cutting, Joe, Thompson-Lee, Sophie, Snell, Rebecca J.S., See, Beng Huat, Saiger, Michael. (2025). Digital innovations in teacher recruitment: An experimental study. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105450
